card.hook: Black lava, milky blue water and steam drifting over the top: the Blue Lagoon looks like a movie set, and it's built to be photographed. Even better, it's man-made, so you can say you've been to Iceland's most famous swimming pool.
card.stand_here: Stand about 10 m south of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. Stay on the paths and in the areas open to visitors.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to fit in the whole lagoon, the lava and Mount Þorbjörn. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, more natural look, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out people in the water, swirls of steam or the edge of the lava.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the water, then drag the slider to make the picture a little darker so the pale blue keeps its colour and the white steam doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: An overcast day gives soft, even light that suits the milky blue. Low sun early or late adds warmth and shadows on the lava. In the dark months, use night mode and rest your phone against a rail or wall to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Head for the wooden walkway that runs out to the hexagonal platform floating on the water. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and let the steaming blue water fill the space behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine in the lagoon itself but not in the locker rooms. Phones and cameras aren't allowed at all in the Retreat Spa and Retreat Lagoon, so use the main pool area. A waterproof case is a smart idea, because a phone dropped in the milky water can be damaged and is hard to find. Check the official site for current opening and access before you go.
card.challenge: Be patient and wait for a gap in the steam, then snap the moment the blue breaks through.
card.good_to_know: The water is a by-product of the nearby Svartsengi geothermal power station, and its milky blue colour comes from the silica in it. Bathing facilities opened in 1987, and it's now one of the most visited attractions in Iceland. Lava reached the site in November 2024 and destroyed the car park, but protective barriers kept the lagoon itself intact.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 10 m south of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. Stay on the paths and in the areas open to visitors.

selfie_research.safety: Carry the phone in a waterproof case, since a dropped phone in the milky water can be damaged and is hard to find.
selfie_research.notes: Only blogs and a few guides were found; no page names a spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole lagoon and building in frame, so ask_someone_spot is null. The walkway and platform are described without a formal name, so check on a map before going. The jasminealley page mentions a popular photo spot just outside the changing-room exit, but it is described only by position, not by a mappable name, so I left it out. Most sources are several years old, and the area near Grindavík has had volcanic disruption, so check current access and conditions with the operator before visiting.

card.hook: Most Reykjanes stops are about empty lava and sky. Grindavík adds boats, working quays and low roofs sitting on an old lava field, so your photo says something about life here.
card.stand_here: Stand on Grindavíkurhöfn, the working harbour waterfront, with the boats and harbour buildings in front of you. The town is about 7 minutes on foot (580 m) to the north-west. Face the boats and rooftops with the wide sky behind them.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to show the town as you see it. Try 0.5x if you want more sky and landscape, then 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a boat or the lighthouse in the distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower third line, with the rooftops and boats in the middle band.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer, lower light on the buildings and landscape. Around midday on a bright day the sky can look washed out.
card.selfie_here: Head to the harbour quay beside the Bryggjan restaurant and use the front camera with the moored fishing boats over your shoulder. Try 0.5x to squeeze in more of the harbour behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The town has been affected by volcanic activity since late 2023, so check safetravel.is before you go, as access can change at short notice. Keep to signs and closures, stay on marked paths and off open ground because crevasses can be expected, and don't cross barriers for a better angle.
card.challenge: Find a spot where a boat, a rooftop and a strip of lava ground all fit in one shot, with the sky taking up at least half the picture.
card.good_to_know: Grindavík is a working fishing town, and its harbour, Hópið, only became the fishing base in 1939, when locals dug a channel through a reef to reach the sea. A lighthouse built in 1928 stands on the southern tip of the nearby peninsula. The Blue Lagoon is about 5 kilometres away.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Grindavíkurhöfn, the working harbour waterfront, with the boats and harbour buildings in front of you. The town is about 7 minutes on foot (580 m) to the north-west. Face the boats and rooftops with the wide sky behind them.

selfie_research.safety: Stay on marked paths and off open ground, because crevasses can be expected in Grindavík.
selfie_research.notes: Grindavík is a town in recovery, not a conventional photo stop. Sources say it is open, but access can change at short notice and some areas are restricted, so check safetravel.is before going. No page names a spot where the whole town is framed behind a visitor, so the harbour is the best documented option, not a verified viewpoint. No page describes a passer-by framing spot, so ask_someone_spot is null. Hópsnesviti lighthouse is a photo stop just outside town, but no page places it as a view of Grindavík itself, so I left it out. One guide says visitors should not treat damaged neighbourhoods as photo opportunities, and another asks visitors not to look into windows of abandoned houses or walk through yards, so I avoided the cracked streets and lava-damaged areas. No page gives selfie stick or tripod rules.

card.hook: You're rolling into Grindavík and there's a big lump of mountain sitting right beside the road, all on its own. Þorbjörn is only 243 m, but with nothing crowding it, it fills your phone screen like it's posing.
card.stand_here: Stand on Grindavíkurvegur, on the stretch heading into Grindavík from the Blue Lagoon side. Face north-west toward the mountain so it rises beside the road, and use a safe verge or pull-in, never the road itself.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the road, the mountain and the sky all fit. Try 0.5x only if you want lots of foreground, because it makes the mountain look smaller. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) picks out the summit buildings and the ridge line.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the mountain on one third of the frame and let the road lead the eye in, keeping the horizon level.
card.best_time: Go when the sun is low, in the early morning or the hours before sunset, so the slopes show some shape. Flat midday light makes the mountain look a bit dull.
card.selfie_here: If you're visiting the Blue Lagoon, stand on the lagoon's shoreline with Þorbjörn behind you, since the lagoon sits in a lava field in front of the mountain. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and hold the phone a bit low so the mountain stays over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: On the road stretch from the Blue Lagoon toward Grindavík, ask your helper to shoot from a safe verge or pull-in, away from traffic, with the mountain rising behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The mountain has seen ground movement and earthquakes since 2020, and magma is accumulating near the Svartsengi area right next to it. Check the hazard assessment and current access and closure notices before you set off, and before any walk up the mountain.
card.challenge: Get a road-and-mountain shot with no cars in it. Take a few tries, because traffic loves to wander into the frame at the last second.
card.good_to_know: Þorbjörn grew from eruptions under a glacier during a cold spell in the Pleistocene. A long split across the top forms a small canyon up to 80 m deep, called Þjófagjá, or Thieves' Canyon, after an old story of bandits caught by a farmer's son. The jeep track up the slope was built by the U.S. Army during World War II.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Grindavíkurvegur, on the stretch heading into Grindavík from the Blue Lagoon side. Face north-west toward the mountain so it rises beside the road, and use a safe verge or pull-in, never the road itself.

selfie_spots.why: A page describes the lagoon as lying in front of the mountain, and a photo taken from the lagoon shows Þorbjörn in the background.

selfie_research.safety: Check the hazard assessment before setting off, since the peak lies right next to the Svartsengi area, where magma is accumulating.
selfie_research.notes: Only one selfie spot was supported by the pages found. The summit (reached by a trail from Nesvegur/Grindavíkurvegur, with a radio tower and small buildings) was not used as a selfie spot because the mountain would be underfoot, not behind. The 'ask someone' location is a road stretch, not a named pull-off, so the exact stopping point is unverified. Sources conflict on direction: one says the mountain is on the left after leaving the Blue Lagoon, another says it is on the right on the road to Grindavík. No page gave selfie stick or tripod rules. The volcanic situation is changing, so check current access and hazard advice before going.

card.hook: Picture steam drifting up from pipes and buildings, with nothing around them but black lava and a huge sky. That's Svartsengi, and the odd mix is exactly why it looks so good on your phone.
card.stand_here: Head for the spot near Norðurljósavegur and stand about 350 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face south-east and the plant is in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole scene in. Then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the pipes, chimneys and steam. Use 0.5x only if you can get dark rock or a path in the foreground.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on the top or bottom third line, then tap the buildings and slide a little darker so the sky and steam keep their detail.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the sun is low, is the time to aim for. It gives the buildings and steam more shape.
card.selfie_here: Try the shore of the cooling lake in front of the plant, where the plant stands across the water. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the steam and pipework over your shoulder. Dusk, when the plant's lights come on, is suggested as a lovely time. We don't know the exact spot to stand, so wander along the edge until the plant sits nicely behind you.
card.ask_someone: Find the roadside verge facing the plant, where a passer-by can pull over safely, and stand between them and the plant so the whole site is behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay out of restricted zones, don't step onto fresh lava, and don't treat damaged areas as photo opportunities. This is a working plant in an area hit by volcanic activity, so view it from a public place and check vedur.is and almannavarnir.is before you go.
card.challenge: Get three layers in one shot: dark ground at the bottom, buildings in the middle, steam and sky on top, with the horizon dead level.
card.good_to_know: Svartsengi means 'black meadow', which suits the setting. The plant opened in 1976 and was the world's first to combine electricity with hot water for district heating. Its hot water heats more than 21,000 households on the Reykjanes Peninsula, and the Blue Lagoon is a spin-off of the same geothermal field.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the spot near Norðurljósavegur and stand about 350 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face south-east and the plant is in front of you.

Sources disagree on access: the Visit Reykjanes and Iceland Spirit pages say Grindavík or the Blue Lagoon is open, while a page dated 7 days ago says Grindavík has no current visitor all-clear and that Svartsengi is in the moderate hazard category. The Icelandic Meteorological Office alert level is 2 (orange) per an update dated 27 October 2026. Check vedur.is and almannavarnir.is before going. No page stated selfie stick or tripod rules.
